documentGuides.title: Birth certificate
documentGuides.summary: Usually the first one to get. Most other papers ask to see it.

sections.heading: How to get it
items: Order it from the Georgia Department of Public Health. You can order online, and the state's page also lists other ways to request it.
Only the person named on the certificate (or a close family member) can order it. Say who you are and where you were born.
You'll need to show proof of who you are. Photos of an ID on your phone are not accepted.
If you were born in another state, order from that state's vital records office instead.

sections.heading: Cost and time
items: About $25 for each certified copy, plus about $8 for online processing.
It can take up to 10 weeks by regular mail. Faster shipping costs extra (about $16 online).

sections.heading: Good to know
items: No ID yet? Ask your outreach worker or case manager. They can often help with the request, or with the fee.
Ask for a "certified copy". That's the kind offices accept.

links.label: Georgia Department of Public Health: ways to request a record

documentGuides.title: Social Security card
documentGuides.summary: Free to replace. You can get a new one even if you don't remember the number.

sections.heading: How to get it
items: Fill out the Social Security card form (Form SS-5). It's free.
Bring it, with one paper that proves who you are, to your local Social Security office. Find yours with the office locator.
If you have a Georgia driver's license or state ID and a mailing address, you may be able to do it online with a "my Social Security" account.
The new card comes in the mail in about 10 business days.

sections.heading: Cost and limits
items: It costs nothing. Social Security never charges for a card.
You can get up to 3 replacement cards a year and 10 in your lifetime.

sections.heading: Good to know
items: They need a mailing address to send the card. Ask your outreach worker if a trusted place can receive mail for you.
Asking for a card at a Social Security office is free. Be careful of anyone who asks you to pay.

links.label: Apply online with my Social Security

documentGuides.title: Georgia photo ID
documentGuides.summary: Get your birth certificate and Social Security card first. The ID office asks for them.

sections.heading: How to get it
items: Go to a Department of Driver Services (DDS) office and ask for an ID card.
Bring proof of who you are, your Social Security number, that you're a U.S. citizen or here legally, and where you live.
For where you live, DDS accepts a letter from a shelter or care provider where you're staying. It must be on their official letterhead.
DDS lists exactly which papers it accepts on its website. Check before you go.

sections.heading: Cost
items: A regular Georgia ID costs about $32.
Can't pay? Ask about the Indigent ID Card. You get a voucher from an approved nonprofit, then take it to DDS. Ask your outreach worker if they can give you one.

sections.heading: Good to know
items: A free voter ID card is also available if you're registered to vote.
Once you have it, add it to your vault so a copy is always with you.

links.label: DDS: get an Indigent ID Card

documentGuides.title: Veteran discharge papers (DD-214)
documentGuides.summary: Free to request. It opens the door to VA health care and housing help.

sections.heading: How to get it
items: Request it from the National Archives. The easiest way is online with eVetRecs.
Or mail in Standard Form 180 (SF-180) to the National Personnel Records Center.
Have ready: your full name, your branch, your dates of service, and your service number or Social Security number.

sections.heading: Cost
items: It's free for veterans and their next of kin.

sections.heading: Good to know
items: Homeless veterans can call the VA's national helpline any time for housing and health help.
Mail address: National Personnel Records Center, Military Personnel Records, 1 Archives Drive, St. Louis, MO 63138.

links.label: National Archives: request military service records

phones.label: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans

benefitPrograms.title: Medicaid
benefitPrograms.summary: Free or low-cost health coverage. In Georgia it depends on your situation.

sections.heading: Who can get it
items: Children, parents with low income, pregnant women, older adults, and people with a qualifying disability.
Georgia has not expanded Medicaid to every low-income adult. A single adult with no children may not qualify unless they use the Pathways program.

Georgia Pathways to Coverage is for adults 19 to 64 with no minor children and very low income (about $15,960 a year for one person in 2026). It normally asks for 80 hours a month of work, training, school or certain caregiving.
Temporary homelessness can count as a "good cause" to be excused from the 80 hours. Ask when you apply.
People who get SSI are generally covered.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Apply on Georgia Gateway (online), or ask your outreach worker or a health center to help you.
You don't need a permanent address to apply.

sections.heading: Have ready
items: Photo ID, Social Security number, proof of income (or a note that you have none), and a mailing address.

benefitPrograms.title: Low-cost clinics in Savannah
benefitPrograms.summary: See a doctor, dentist or counselor for a fee based on your income, even with no insurance.

sections.heading: Where to go
items: Curtis V. Cooper Primary Health Care is a community health center for Savannah and Chatham County. It offers checkups, behavioral health, pharmacy and dental care, with discounts based on income and family size.
J.C. Lewis Primary Health Care Center was started by Union Mission to care for people who are homeless.

sections.heading: Good to know
items: Community health centers see people whether or not they can pay.
Ask about the "sliding fee" or "discount" program when you call or check in.
Bring any ID or insurance card you have, but don't stay away if you have none.

links.label: Curtis V. Cooper Primary Health Care
Free and low-cost clinics in Chatham County

benefitPrograms.title: Insurance plans with help paying
benefitPrograms.summary: Private health plans with lower prices for people with low income.

sections.heading: Who can get it
items: Adults with low or no income can often get a plan with a big discount on the monthly cost.
There is usually a sign-up period each year. Some life changes, like losing coverage, open a chance to sign up at other times.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Go to Georgia Access, or ask a local helper (called a "navigator") to sit down with you and do it together.

benefitPrograms.title: Medicare
benefitPrograms.summary: For people 65 and older, and some people with disabilities.

sections.heading: Who can get it
items: People 65 or older who have worked enough, and people who have received Social Security disability (SSDI) for 24 months.
If you have low income, help paying the monthly cost may be available.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Apply with Social Security, or call and ask.

benefitPrograms.title: VA health care for veterans
benefitPrograms.summary: Health care, mental health care and housing help for veterans. Homeless veterans get priority help.

sections.heading: Who can get it
items: Most veterans who served on active duty and did not receive a dishonorable discharge.
HUD-VASH pairs a housing voucher with a VA case manager for homeless veterans.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Apply online at VA.gov, call, or visit a VA medical center.
Have your DD-214 discharge papers if you can. If you don't have them, see "Replace a document".

phones.label: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans

benefitPrograms.title: Hospital bills
benefitPrograms.summary: Nonprofit hospitals must have a way to reduce or wipe out bills for people who can't pay.

sections.heading: What to do
items: Ask the hospital for "financial assistance" or "charity care" and for the application.
Ask before you pay anything. You can often apply even after you've been treated.
Keep the papers they give you. Your outreach worker can help fill it out.

benefitPrograms.title: Food help (SNAP and WIC)
benefitPrograms.summary: Monthly money for groceries, and extra food help for young families.

sections.heading: Who can get it
items: SNAP helps people with low income buy food. You don't need a permanent address to apply.
WIC is for pregnant women, new mothers, babies, and children under 5.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Apply for SNAP on Georgia Gateway. Tell them if you have almost no money right now, since that can speed things up.
For WIC, contact the Chatham County health department.

benefitPrograms.title: Mental health and crisis help
benefitPrograms.summary: Someone is there to talk any time, day or night.

sections.heading: Right now
items: If you or someone else is in danger, call 911.
If you're in crisis or thinking about hurting yourself, call or text 988. It's free and open all day and night.

sections.heading: Ongoing care
items: Community health centers, like Curtis V. Cooper, offer counseling and help with substance use on a sliding fee.
Ask your outreach worker to connect you with a counselor.
